article_text:
冨永愛の伝統to未来 第二章～ニッポンの伝統文化を未来へ紡ぐ～

サブタイトル：小千谷縮

放送日時：2026年10月21日(水)夜10時～10時30分

放送局：BS日テレ

出演者：冨永愛

クレジット：ⒸＢＳ日テレ

番組概要:冨永愛が全国各地を訪ね、その土地に根付く「伝統文化」を紹介します。先人たちから受け継がれてきた「伝統」の素晴らしさを伝えるとともに、後継者問題など伝統文化が置かれている「現状」、そして進むべき「未来」を探っていきます。

番組ホームページ： https://www.bs4.jp/dentotomirai/ 番組公式X： https://x.com/dentou_mirai 番組公式Youtube: https://www.youtube.com/@dentoumirai 番組公式TikTok： https://www.tiktok.com/@dentoumirai 番組公式インスタグラム： https://www.instagram.com/bs4_dentou_mirai/

手作業で作り上げる肌触りと着心地

今回の舞台は、新潟県小千谷市。信濃川が流れ、冬には深い雪に包まれるこの街は、古くから織物の産地として知られています。

この街で作られてきたのは「小千谷縮」。表面に「シボ」と呼ばれる細かなしわを生み出すことで、さらりとした肌触りと涼しい着心地が特徴。1本1本の繊維から手作業で作り上げる昔ながらの製法の小千谷紬はユネスコの無形文化遺産にも登録されています。

気の遠くなる作業の連続 一本の糸を布に

今回は愛さんが、繊維業界を目指す国際トータルファッション専門学校の学生さんと一緒に、小千谷が織物の街になった理由と、小千谷縮の魅力を紐解きます。

小千谷の織物の歴史や技術を学べる体験型の織物ギャラリー「織之座」では、小千谷織物同業協同組合の理事長・高橋さんに、産地の成り立ちを伺います。

小千谷縮の工房「耶麻工房」では、一本の糸が布になるまでに、どれほどの手間と技が込められているのか？その理由に迫ります。また、雪にさらすことで生地を漂白する「雪さらし」とは？

そして、愛さんと学生さんが、絣模様の染色とわずかな職人しかできない織に挑戦！わずかでも位置がずれると、柄全体がずれてしまったり、1000本ある経糸が切れてしまうという職人技に挑戦。 愛さんもたじろいだ結果は?

新しいファッションも登場

さらに、今年開催された「TGC新潟2026」では、小千谷紬や十日町友禅など着物をリメイクした衣装がランウェイに登場。受け継がれてきた織物や染めの技が、学生たちの発想で新しいファッションへと生まれ変わりました。

十日町友禅を手がけた老舗「関芳」。ここで発展した金や銀の輝きで柄を彩る金彩友禅の加工の様子も紹介します。

(美術展ナビ編集班)

Paramount’s Street Fighter fought off Universal animation Forgotten Island to top the UK-Ireland box office, as Bollywood action title Jailer 2 made the top five on opening weekend.

Kitao Sakurai’s Street Fighter opened to £2.3m from 594 locations, at a £3,872 average. That tops the £1.6m opening of fellow martial arts video game film Mortal Kombat 2 from May. The latter title went on to a £3.4m total; Street Fighter will look to beat that within the next week then move towards £5m.

Street Fighter ’s opening was up on the £619,000 opening of the 1995 film of the same name, and only slightly behind its £2.3m total; it may yet pass it with final weekend figures still to come (figures are not adjusted for inflation).

Universal’s DreamWorks animation Forgotten Island opened to £1.3m from 628 sites at a £2,072 average. That is down on the £1.7m start of the latest DreamWorks title, Gabby’s Dollhouse: The Movie , from the equivalent weekend last year, but up on the £885,000 start of the last DreamWorks film not based on pre-existing material, 2023’s Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken .

Amazon MGM Studios’ latest Colleen Hoover adaptation Verity added £1.1m on its third weekend, falling just one place. Its 44% drop brought it to £9.5m total, well clear of the £6.3m of last year’s Regretting You and £4.5m of this year’s Reminders Of Him among Hoover adaptations, although still behind the £21.9m of 2024’s It Ends With Us . Sony handles the theatrical release.

Last weekend’s number one Other Mommy dropped 54% on its second weekend for Universal, with £924,000 taking it to a £3.8m total.

Bollywood action sequel Jailer 2 , about a retired police officer whose life is disrupted when a criminal organisation threatens his family, opened to £754,000 from just 230 sites at a healthy £3,365 average, up on the £728,000 start of the first film in 2023. Jailer 2 has £1.2m already including previews, and will hope to top the £1.3m cume of the first film this week, for distributor TGS Cinemas, with bookings by Boleyn Cinema.

Takings for the top five increased by 3% on last weekend with £6.3m, and are 18% up on the equivalent weekend last year, with a decent spread of titles bringing in money. Next weekend also has a broad spread of genres starting out, including Black Bear stop motion animation Wildwood , Warner Bros’ comic book adaptation Clayface , Lionsgate TV spin off Ghosts: The Possession Of Button House , Amazon MGM Studios’ Ali G: Who Iz I? , and Sony’s literary adaptation Klara And The Sun .

Whalefall opens up

Trafalgar Releasing’s Greek myths-inspired Hadestown: The Musical did a healthy £627,000 from 542 sites at a £1,157 average, and has £1.5m in total having opened on Tuesday, October 13.

Disney opened Brian Duffield’s survival thriller Whalefall to £508,000 at a £1,015 average from 500 locations.

Heart Of The Beast starring Brad Pitt fell 38% on its fourth weekend for Paramount, continuing its healthy box office run. It is up to £6.4m lifetime.

Resident Evil is continuing its successful box office run towards Halloween, adding £477,000 – a 39% drop – and hitting £13.6m for Sony.

Source: Focus Features LLC

‘Sense And Sensibility’

Sense And Sensibility starring Daisy Edgar-Jones added £310,000 on its fourth weekend for Universal, falling 48% and reaching £5.9m total.

Facebook drama The Social Reckoning put on £284,000 on its second weekend for Sony, a 54% fall that brought it to a flat £1.3m total.

Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom leads Studiocanal’s slate, with £257,000 on its fifth session, down 48% on the previous session. The stop-motion animation is up to £4.2m total.

Warner Bros’ Digger starring Tom Cruise took a bigger hit from its second to third weekend than on the previous session. It dropped 62% this time, with £184,000 taking it to £2.3m total.

NAZA , the documentary about Israeli military techniques used to kill Palestinians in Gaza, started with an impressive £173,000 from just 51 sites at a £3,395 average, one of the highest of the weekend. The film, distributed in cinemas by Dogwoof ahead of its free launch on The Guardian website in late November, has £240,000 including previews, and was the number one title in 40 of its 51 sites.

article_text:
Art Review

When Does a Woman Artist Reach Her "Prime"?

"The Prime of Your Life" examines what recognition and market success mean for 18 women artists over 75.

“What is an ‘old-age style’? Is it the same as a ‘late style’?” asks Linda Nochlin at the start of her 2008 essay, “Old-Age Style: Late Louise Bourgeois.” As our understanding of an artwork evolves with the artist’s age, the essay examines Bourgeois’s enduring aesthetics and interests throughout her seven-decade career, focusing particularly on the soft and hard qualities of her work. Nochlin, the esteemed feminist art historian, meditates on the relationship between a work made early in an artist’s career and one made at the end of their life, asking how the latter changes our understanding or interpretation of the former. Borrowing from the late Palestinian-American literary theorist Edward Said, Nochlin concludes that “late styles abandon all the comforting segues and aesthetic connections that hold the art object together, dealing instead with disconnects, abysses, unyielding dislocation and unresolved contradiction.” Late styles, in other words, force us to contend with shifts and disruptions in artistic focus, whether tied to an artist’s biography or not, that don’t fit neatly into historical assessments of earlier work.

Nochlin’s definition of “late style” is helpful in understanding The Prime of Your Life , on view at Marc Straus Gallery in New York. Gathering 18 women artists over the age of 75, the exhibition is a cacophony of materials, concerns, and, yes, styles. Painting, drawing, sculpture, and installation, in wildly different scales, forms, and techniques, all congregate as a series of calls and responses rather than unified harmony. With only their age assembling them, the works in this exhibition offer less of a generational statement and more a critical question of 21st-century feminist art history: What does “prime” mean for a woman artist, when their work is most likely to be valorized by the market and museums only in their older age?

The Prime of Your Life at Marc Straus Gallery, New York

Marina Abramović’s photograph “Standing with Skeleton” (2008/2016) introduces this question. Installed near the gallery’s entrance, the large-scale image depicts Abramović in black against an equally inky background with an ivory skeleton atop her back. Over 50 years, she has almost always used her body in her performance-driven work, eschewing subtlety for straight-on confrontation. She did this poetically with her 2010 epic performance and exhibition The Artist is Present , regarded as a career zenith, in which she stared opposite another individual during museum hours. Compared with the rigor and passion of Abramović's live performances, this photograph feels, at best, inanimate, and at worst, almost like a parody of her practice; the skeleton seems more like lighthearted Halloween decor than an elegiac meditation on old age. Does knowing the strength of Abramović's other work make this look like a comic pastiche? Is it fair to compare? Does a lesser, later work diminish the strength of the stronger, more provocative and innovative earlier one? How will we know if "Standing with Skeleton" is a late work? Perhaps now, at 79, Abramović is just hitting her prime, an epoch of work on the horizon.

article_text:
La representante de RJ Mitte confirmó este martes que el actor, reconocido mundialmente por interpretar a Walter “Flynn” White Jr. en Breaking Bad , murió por suicidio el lunes 12 de octubre en su residencia de Brownsville, Texas. El artista tenía 34 años.

Según informó el Departamento de Policía de Brownsville (BPD), los agentes recibieron una llamada alrededor de las 12:50 del mediodía, hora local, y encontraron al intérprete sin vida en su domicilio. En un primer comunicado, las autoridades habían señalado que la causa y la manera de la muerte permanecían pendientes mientras avanzaba la investigación.

“Es con profunda tristeza que compartimos el trágico fallecimiento del querido actor, filántropo y apasionado defensor de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad RJ Mitte”, expresó su representante en un comunicado sobre el actor de Breaking Bad . Luego, se conoció que el intérprete decidió quitarse la vida .

RJ Mitte, el actor que interpretó al hijo de Walter White en Breaking Bad

Mitte alcanzó reconocimiento internacional gracias a su participación en Breaking Bad , la aclamada producción creada por Vince Gilligan que se emitió por AMC entre 2008 y 2013. A lo largo de sus cinco temporadas, el actor apareció en 56 de los 62 episodios de la serie, en los que interpretó al hijo adolescente de Walter White, el personaje de Bryan Cranston.

El intérprete había sido diagnosticado con parálisis cerebral durante su infancia, una condición que compartía con su personaje . Esa experiencia personal le permitió aportar autenticidad a su actuación y, con el tiempo, convertirse en una voz reconocida en la defensa de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad.

“Partiendo de su propia experiencia viviendo con parálisis cerebral, Mitte aportó autenticidad al papel y construyó una plataforma en torno a la concienciación sobre la discapacidad y la inclusión”, agregó su representante.

Fuera de la pantalla, el actor también desarrolló una importante labor solidaria. Se desempeñó como embajador de United Cerebral Palsy y de Shriners Children’s, además de presidir The Mitte Foundation, una organización dedicada a respaldar iniciativas filantrópicas y comunitarias.

The Mitte Cultural District también le dedicó unas palabras de despedida y lo recordó como un “querido amigo y dedicado defensor de las artes”. La institución destacó su compromiso con Brownsville y el aporte que realizó a la comunidad a través de la cultura.

“Fue un amigo, un socio y alguien que genuinamente creyó en el poder de las artes y la cultura para unir a las personas”, expresó la organización.

Bryan Cranston despidió a RJ Mitte

La noticia generó numerosas muestras de cariño por parte de sus compañeros de Breaking Bad . Bryan Cranston, quien interpretó a su padre en la ficción, compartió un extenso mensaje en redes sociales para recordar al actor y expresar su dolor por la pérdida.

Cranston contó que conoció a Mitte cuando tenía apenas 14 años, luego de que fuera elegido para interpretar a Walter White Jr. En su publicación, destacó la determinación con la que afrontó los desafíos de su condición y el compromiso que mantuvo durante el rodaje.

“Nunca —jamás— permitió que ese desafío fuera una excusa para nada. Afrontó el exigente calendario de rodaje con gran determinación”, escribió el actor.

Sin embargo, uno de los aspectos más dolorosos del mensaje estuvo relacionado con el vínculo que ambos habían mantenido a lo largo de los años, incluso después de que terminara la serie.

“Es especialmente devastador saber que se quitó la vida”, expresó Cranston. “¿Por qué? Nos estábamos enviando mensajes de texto hace apenas unas semanas, buscando cuándo podríamos almorzar juntos”.

El intérprete también reflexionó sobre ese último encuentro que habían intentado organizar y sobre el cariño que sentía por su compañero.

“No sé si ese almuerzo habría cambiado su futuro… Pero sé que lo amé y disfruté plenamente estar con él durante todos esos años en la serie, y después de que el foco de Breaking Bad se apagara… Te voy a extrañar, hijo”, concluyó.

View this post on Instagram

Al final de su publicación, Cranston compartió información sobre la línea 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, destinada a brindar asistencia a personas que atraviesan una crisis en Estados Unidos, y dejó un mensaje de esperanza.

También hicieron lo propio Norris, Paul y Esposito

Dean Norris , quien interpretó a Hank Schrader en la ficción, también expresó su tristeza por la muerte de Mitte. El actor recordó el vínculo que había construido con él durante las grabaciones y el cariño con el que lo acompañó desde sus primeros años en el set.

“Estoy destrozado. Aunque RJ no interpretaba a mi hijo en la ficción, siempre lo cuidé como a un chico joven en el set. Era un joven de buen corazón y se lo va a extrañar mucho. Esto es tan desgarrador, no puedo creerlo. Pienso en él y en su familia”, escribió.

View this post on Instagram

Por su parte, Aaron Paul , quien dio vida a Jesse Pinkman, manifestó estar “sin palabras” tras conocer la noticia y le dedicó un mensaje a su compañero.

“Estoy destrozado por esta noticia. RJ, te quiero, amigo mío. Te vamos a extrañar. Y a quien esté leyendo esto: sepan que son amados y que no están solos. Recuérdenlo siempre”, expresó.

“Querido uno, No hay palabras que puedan expresar lo que tu amistad ha significado para mí. Recordaré la risa, el éxtasis de pura alegría en los momentos amorosos que hemos compartido. Recordaré la magnitud de tu bondad, tu filantropía, tu estar al servicio de los demás antes que a ti mismo. ¡Por siempre vivirás en mi corazón, representando cómo el amor puro puede cambiar el mundo! Descansa en paz. Ahora eres libre. Vuela con los ángeles”, sostuvo Giancarlo Esposito.

View this post on Instagram

La muerte de RJ Mitte deja un profundo dolor entre sus compañeros y seguidores de Breaking Bad , una serie que marcó su carrera y lo convirtió en una figura reconocida por su trabajo artístico y su compromiso con la inclusión.

Daily Newsletter

Au Revoir, Art Basel Paris

French museums and galleries are shuttering before nationwide protests tomorrow. Plus: What does it mean for a woman artist to “reach her prime”?

Leave it to Art Basel Paris to close early during a movement for education equality and working conditions … “in the interest of safeguarding our visitors.” The Louvre, Gagosian, and other museums and galleries also announced plans to shutter during tomorrow’s nationwide protests. One artist coalition calls the fair’s cancellation a victory for the fight to defend culture: “Let us keep the movement going.” Staff Writers Anna Lee and Rhea Nayyar have the story.

Across the pond, Ed Simon reflects on the imperative to protect arts and culture here in the United States on the centenary of the University of Pittsburgh’s Cathedral of Learning, founded as a beacon of education and expression that “seems virtually utopian today.” Then, we have the artists keeping that spirit alive: Read on for Leah Triplett Harrington’s review of a show that deconstructs sexist notions of recognition and market success for women artists over age 75, the painter who adorns Phoebe Bridgers’s guitars, and more.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

Meet the Painter Adorning Phoebe Bridgers’s Guitars

On an average day in December 2022, the Pasadena-based surrealist classicist painter John Griswold got an Instagram DM from musician Phoebe Bridgers.

“I remember she said ‘big fan,’” Griswold told Hyperallergic , “and I thought that was pretty funny, given the fact that, to quote a common epithet of hers, she’s ‘Phoebe Fucking Bridgers.’”

The indie darling went on to ask Griswold if he had ever painted on a guitar, and from there a collaborative artistic relationship was born. | Sophia Lebowitz

The Latest From Paris

Amid ongoing nationwide demonstrations for better living conditions in France, Art Basel Paris says it will close early on October 23 ahead of planned protests on Saturday.

Following the announcement, Art Basel also plans to remove all outdoor sculptures installed on Winston Churchill Avenue .

Several Paris museums including the Louvre, the Musée d’Orsay, the Musée de l’Orangerie, and the Musée National Picasso will be closed on Saturday .

editorial_excerpt_zh: 阿尔伯塔·惠特尔（Alberta Whittle）1980年出生于加勒比海岛国巴巴多斯，现生活和工作于苏格兰格拉斯哥。她多面向的创作实践以发展一种对跨大西洋黑奴贸易遗产的个人回应为核心，揭露其与种族主义……的关联。

"《（非）接纳》，阿尔伯塔·惠特尔，2018年。由艺术家及格拉斯哥Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd.提供", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿尔伯塔·惠特尔1980年出生于加勒比海岛国巴巴多斯，现生活和工作于苏格兰格拉斯哥。她多面向的创作实践以发展一种对跨大西洋黑奴贸易遗产的个人回应为核心，揭露其与当下制度性种族主义、白人至上主义和气候紧急状况的关联。面对压抑的政治语境，惠特尔力图推动希望，以及抵抗、自我照护与集体照护的不同形式。她毕业于爱丁堡艺术学院美术专业，获格拉斯哥艺术学院硕士学位和爱丁堡大学博士学位，现为约翰内斯堡大学研究助理，并曾获保罗·哈姆林基金会奖（2022）、弗里兹艺术家奖（2020）和亨利·摩尔基金会艺术家奖（2020）。2026年初，她在巴西作为Pivô Salvador的驻留艺术家度过了一段时间，其间为当地的节庆与集体仪式所吸引，如里奥韦尔梅柳的伊曼雅节和卡舒埃拉的善终兄弟会的活动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/06.-TMI-WHITA-49882.png?resize=1024%2C725&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "《关于接纳的冥想》，阿尔伯塔·惠特尔，2018年。由艺术家及格拉斯哥Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd.提供", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿尔伯塔·惠特尔游走于录像、行为、摄影、水彩和刺绣等语言之间，而正是在拼贴这一技法中，她不仅找到了最初的创作庇护所，也找到了一把解读其全部多媒体作品的可能的钥匙——这些作品可以被视为由所用过程和所涉主题构成的一幅宏观拼贴。在巴巴多斯的青少年时期，阿尔伯塔饱受慢性疼痛之苦，这促使她与家人迁往英格兰腹地的伯明翰，寻求纤维肌痛的治疗。在这次与17世纪殖民加勒比海岛的英国入侵者方向相反的跨大西洋迁移之前，这位艺术家几乎处于与世隔绝的状态，大部分时间都被困在床上。在房间里，她最喜欢的消遣就是做拼贴、画画和自画像——这些媒介至今仍主导着她的创作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果说四面墙之间的避风港是贴在纸上的图像拼合，那么在户外，始终接纳阿尔伯塔的是海洋的深邃与辽阔。正因如此，在伯明翰之后，她选择苏格兰作为新家，以重新与水域建立联系——水是创造力的源泉，也是贯穿她全部作品的美学与象征元素。海浪也拍打着她2012年至2019年间在南非建立的临时家园——那个地方让她思考世界上黑人处境的共通性。正是在巴巴多斯、约翰内斯堡和开普敦之间辗转的时期，阿尔伯塔重新拾起了青少年时期的庇护式实践。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/05.-TMI-WHITA-49881.png?resize=512%2C1024&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "《不稳定的地图II：一如既往》，出自《一如既往》系列，阿尔伯塔·惠特尔，沙滩巾上的数码印花，2019年。由艺术家及格拉斯哥Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd.提供", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/07.-TMI-WHITA-49883.png?resize=594%2C1024&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "《不稳定的地图I：一如既往》，出自《一如既往》系列，阿尔伯塔·惠特尔，沙滩巾上的数码印花，2019年。由艺术家及格拉斯哥Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd.提供", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "始于2016年的数码拼贴系列《一如既往》（Business as usual）凝聚了阿尔伯塔·惠特尔——一位黑人、酷儿、加勒比与苏格兰女性——的许多形式、象征与传记层面的议题。这一媒介强烈的图像负载适于推动关于移民、归属感和黑人群体权利的讨论，不仅在英国——2018年以“疾风世代”权利被瓦解为标志——也在整个后殖民世界。“在巴巴多斯与苏格兰之间的往返对我开始解构我们如何理解历史、领土和人民，以及如何在我们共同的历史中讲述我们来自何处的故事，非常重要。”因此，许多图像位于出发与抵达之间的阈限空间，而这些空间又成为入侵或欢迎、相遇或告别，或同时兼而有之的背景。对阿尔伯塔而言，拼贴恰恰允许将不同的想法汇聚在一起，同时展示它们的裂隙及其来源，几乎像是揭示其最深的根。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《一如既往》这个标题借用了英语中的一个习语，可大致意译为“生活照旧”或“一如既往”。对这位艺术家而言，这个说法描述了一种尽管周围困难或动荡却持续不变的状态。带着几分讽刺，阿尔伯塔重新挪用了这句安抚性的话语，以指出现状如何保持不变，仿佛什么都没发生，尽管它承载着殖民主义和帝国主义历史以及仍在进行的种族灭绝的残酷后果。通过拼贴讲述这些“艰难”的历史，这位艺术家力图推动对这段仍然如此在场的过去的承认及其疗愈。因此，尽管该系列的大部分作品创作于2016年至2018年间，阿尔伯塔仍强调这是一项仍在进行中的工作，因为正如她的行为作品或集体作品一样，它只有通过与他人的合作才得以完成；更具体地说，正是该系列所引发的对话使它成为一件完整的艺术作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/11.-TMI-WHITA-49879.png?resize=1024%2C724&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "《一如既往》，阿尔伯塔·惠特尔，2018年。由艺术家及格拉斯哥Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd.提供", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "观察构成这一系列的作品，我们会看到相互对照的叠置，既有不同语言（自画像、文字、水彩、照片，以及取自硬盘、书籍或笔记本的图像）的叠置，也有不同性质与时间性的叠置。对这位艺术家而言，目标是“处理剥削与气候殖民主义的历史，因为在相互交错的不同过程与时刻中——在代际与技术之间，尤其关注原住民技术的被根除——仍然持续着一种感觉，仿佛这就是进步。真正让我不安的，正是进步——或所谓的进步——与黑人及原住民技术之间的这种摩擦，因为我觉得，传给我们的知识常常被轻视和忽视。”这种挖掘在形式上产生的成果，是既鲜活又挑衅的构图；在其中，Whittle 自由地将星系与16、17世纪船只的幽灵、火箭与昆虫、Google 的标志与兰花并置。过去、现在与未来被呈现在同一个平面上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种“所谓进步”不同阶段的共存，直接让人想到墨西哥与阿根廷人类学家内斯托尔·加西亚·坎克利尼（Néstor García Canclini）在1990年代末提出、至今仍然切题的概念——异质多时间性（multitemporalidad "睁开的眼睛、海螺、热带水果与海水，是该系列多件拼贴中反复出现、骤然闯入的一些元素。Alberta Whittle 庞大的图像志，汇聚自一种紧迫状态，并被导入一种仪式性、直觉性且身体性的创作过程：“我在生活和实践中大量使用仪式。燃烧的香、点燃的蜡烛……那是反思、疗愈我身体与灵魂的时刻，我会想到我的祖先，想到如何向他们致敬或请求指引。在这种语境中，我的作品变成一种咒语和祭品，用来看看我们共同能够想象出什么，”她透露。因此，构成这份祭品的每一种材料，除了美学价值，也承载着丰富的象征意义。例如，剪下来的眼睛带有观看与被观看的双重意识，而这两种行动依视角不同，可能带有相互矛盾的意涵。从图形角度看，这些器官的重复赋予画面一种“故障”（glitch），一种构图中的噪点——这种手法不仅出现在拼贴中，也出现在 Alberta 的影片里；她不喜欢扁平的表面，而喜欢玩弄肌理，并由此创造图案。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "海螺也是一种兼具图形性与象征性的矛盾元素，既可用作装饰（Alberta 的母亲一直用它们制作首饰），也可作为宗教仪式中的工具，同时它们又与奴隶制历史直接相连——在那段历史中，海螺曾被当作买卖灵魂的交换货币。Alberta 感兴趣的是物件中栖居的这些多重解读层次，以及它们所产生的摩擦。此外，与眼睛并列，海螺也显示出艺术家的感官兴趣：取决于图像的安排，一只海螺可以变成倾听的耳朵，或说话的嘴。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/01.-TMI-WHITA-49733.png?resize=1024%2C725&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "《天界冥想 V》，Alberta Whittle，2018年。由艺术家及格拉斯哥 Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd. 提供。", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "就连艺术家自己的身体也难免矛盾，因此也成为该系列中反复出现的装置。作为一位肤色较浅的加勒比与苏格兰黑人女性，Alberta Whittle 将自己被拍摄的身体投入其中，任由它在参与塑造其身份的不同社群中引发无数解读。在开普敦街头，人们会停下来问这位艺术家是不是德国人；而在英国，同时身为黑人和苏格兰人却被视为一种不可能。因此，对 Alberta 而言，插入自己的形象是一种反思文化混血、反思如何可能同时归属于不止一种身份的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alberta 借出自己的身躯，重演《Business as usual》中的神话与原型。在一些拼贴作品中，可以辨认出自由女神像高傲的姿态——这一独立、民主与希望的象征，其价值与当前美国政府并不合拍——这一矛盾在标题《(UN)welcome》（2018）中被道出（这是对英文联合国缩写“UN”的文字游戏，同时也构成对“welcome”（欢迎）一词的否定）。而在《C.R.E.A.M.》（2017）中，艺术家的发绺化作一窝蛇——直接影射希腊神话中的美杜莎，一个以蛇代发、目光能将胆敢直视者石化的怪物。“我一直着迷于这些女性原型，以及它们如何塑造女性在世界上被看待和对待的方式。对我来说，美杜莎既是一个强有力的象征，也是一个被深深误解的象征。但在我探索这一神话力量的同时，我想用自己的方式来表现它，”Alberta 说道，她为这一神话形象添上一撮加勒比的“sazon”风味，比如90年代 dancehall 文化中典型的蹲姿、椰子和香蕉，还有硬币、纸币和金链。“我带入自己的视角，以便在这些原型中理解自己，思考什么对我有用，用来谈论开采、原住民性、黑人性与女性气质之间的冲突，”她补充道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/13.-TMI-WHITA-49732.png?resize=1024%2C765&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "《I de Ilusão de Inclusão》（包容幻象之 I），Alberta Whittle，2017。由艺术家及格拉斯哥 Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd. 惠允", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "文字是该系列中融入多件拼贴作品的又一元素。对 Alberta 而言，文字是一种手段：尽管它把她带离舒适区、进入诗性实验，却也拉近了她与公众的距离，在注意力分散、误读频发的时代，为她的叙事有力抵达观者搭起一座桥。许多句子——不仅是系列标题，也是每件作品的标题——都带着既讽刺又政治化的语调。其中，一场与字母表的游戏引导着作品的阅读，例如《C is for colonial fantasy》（“C 代表殖民幻想”）或《I is for the Illusion of Inclusion》（“I 代表包容幻象”）。在其他情况下，它们则像祈祷或咒语：I wrap myself in rainbows / protection from your gaze（“我将自己裹入彩虹／免受你目光的侵扰”）。无论是戏谑还是仪式性的，这些文字都直指艺术家所问题化的紧迫议题核心。图像与文字相互补充、彼此强化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/02.-TMI-WHITA-49734.png?resize=1024%2C725&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "《Meditações celestes II》（天界冥想 II），Alberta Whittle，2017。由艺术家及格拉斯哥 Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd. 惠允", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过图像元素、文字与自身形象的非常规并置，Alberta Whittle 试图唤起一种新的未来观念、一种新的在世方式，远离采掘主义、资本主义及其所造成的不平等。通往这种关怀式未来性的道路，在于重新拾起黑人群体、黑人女性——用艺术家的话说，“全球多数女性”——所继承的仪式。在此意义上，作为供品的拼贴作品是门户，邀请人们放慢脚步，停下来倾听祖先——他们可能来自过去、现在，甚至未来——并向他们（或者更确切地说，向她们）学习如何促进疗愈与希望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“对我来说，艺术是一种希望的实践。面对如此多坏消息带来的普遍麻木，我更愿意让能量继续流动。尽管我的许多作品诞生于痛苦、挫败、愤怒与悲伤之地，但在这种对话、诚实与脆弱的交换中，希望得以更新与分享。我们不能停滞不前。让事物保持流动，这些作品就是希望的咒语。”通过这一系列，Alberta Whittle 以低语呐喊：不能再继续 business as usual，不能再像往常一样过日子。通过艺术所激发的魅惑与反思，想象并建造其他未来是可能的。Axé！///", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Marina Dias Teixeira 是常驻圣保罗的编辑、策展人和文化记者，毕业于伦敦艺术大学媒体与文化研究专业。她尤其关注非洲侨民艺术与拉丁美洲艺术，编辑了约20本书，其中包括《Pinacoteca de São Paulo 120 Anos》和《Máquina de Ritmo: Som e Música na Arte Brasileira》，并担任后者的组织者。她为艺术、设计与建筑类媒体撰稿，同时也开展自己的策展项目，如2026年举办的展览《Fio Condutor》。", "translated": true}]

Sua prática multifacetada tem como cerne o desenvolvimento de uma resposta pessoal às heranças do tráfico negreiro transatlântico, desmascarando suas conexões com o racismo institucional, a supremacia branca e a emergência climática no presente. Frente a um contexto político opressivo, Whittle busca promover esperança e diferentes formas de resistência, autocuidado e cuidado coletivo. Formada em Belas Artes pelo Edinburgh College of Art, com mestrado pela Glasgow School of Art e doutorado pela University of Edinburgh, atua como Research Associate na University of Johannesburg e já recebeu prêmios como o Paul Hamlyn Foundation Award (2022), o Frieze Artist Award (2020) e o Henry Moore Foundation Artist Award (2020). No começo de 2026, passou uma temporada no Brasil como artista residente do Pivô Salvador, onde se encantou com festividades e rituais coletivos, como a festa de Iemanjá no Rio Vermelho e as atividades da Irmandade da Boa Morte em Cachoeira."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/06.-TMI-WHITA-49882.png?resize=1024%2C725&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Meditações sobre o acolhimento, de Alberta Whittle, 2018. Cortesia da artista e do Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd., Glasgow", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Transitando entre linguagens como vídeo, performance, fotografia, aquarela e bordado, é na técnica da colagem que Alberta Whittle encontra não só seu primeiro refúgio criativo, mas também uma possível chave de leitura do conjunto de sua obra multimídia, que pode ser vista como uma macrocolagem de processos empregados e temas abordados. Na adolescência em Barbados, Alberta sofreu com dores crônicas que a levaram a se mudar, junto à família, para Birmingham, no coração da Inglaterra, em busca de uma cura para a fibromialgia. Antes dessa migração transatlântica de sentido inverso ao dos invasores britânicos que colonizaram a ilha caribenha no século 17, a artista vivia quase em isolamento, relegada à cama na maior parte do tempo. As ondas oceânicas também lambiam o lar temporário que estabeleceu, entre 2012 e 2019, na África do Sul – lugar que a levou a refletir sobre a condição compartilhada de negritude no mundo. Foi em um período de trânsito entre Barbados, Joanesburgo e Cidade do Cabo que Alberta retomou a prática-refúgio da adolescência."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/05.-TMI-WHITA-49881.png?resize=512%2C1024&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Mapas da precariedade II: Lo de siempre , da série Como de costume , de Alberta Whittle, impressão digital em toalha de praia, 2019. Cortesia da artista e do Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd., Glasgow", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Iniciada em 2016, a série de colagens digitais Business as usual ( Como de costume ) encapsula muitas das questões formais, simbólicas e biográficas de Alberta Whittle, mulher negra, queer , caribenha e escocesa. A forte carga imagética do meio se presta a fomentar discussões sobre migração, pertencimento e direitos da população negra, não apenas no Reino Unido, marcado em 2018 pelo desmonte dos direitos da Geração Windrush [1], mas também em todo o mundo pós-colonial. “O trânsito entre Barbados e Escócia foi muito importante para eu começar a desconstruir como entendemos a história, o território e as pessoas, e de que forma contar as estórias de onde viemos, dentro de nossa história compartilhada”. Por isso, muitas das imagens se situam em espaços limiares entre partida e chegada que, por sua vez, se tornam pano de fundo para invasões ou boas-vindas, encontros ou despedidas, ou tudo ao mesmo tempo. Para Alberta, a colagem permite justamente reunir diferentes ideias, ao passo que mostra suas fissuras e de onde elas vêm, quase como se revelasse suas raízes mais profundas."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "O título Business as usual pega emprestada uma expressão idiomática da língua inglesa, que pode ser traduzida livremente para o português como “vida que segue” ou “como de costume”. Para a artista, a frase descreve uma situação contínua e imutável, apesar das dificuldades ou perturbações ao redor. Com uma boa dose de sarcasmo, Alberta se reapropria da fala apaziguadora para endereçar a maneira como o status quo se mantém inalterado, como se nada fosse, ainda que carregado de consequências brutais das histórias colonialistas e imperialistas e dos genocídios ainda em curso. Ao falar sobre essas histórias “difíceis” por meio de suas colagens, a artista busca promover o reconhecimento desse passado ainda tão presente e sua cura. Por isso, ainda que a maior parte das obras da série se situe entre 2016 e 2018, Alberta reforça que esse é um trabalho ainda em curso, pois, assim como em suas performances ou obras coletivas, ele só se conclui a partir da colaboração com o outro; mais especificamente, são as conversas que a série desperta que a tornam uma obra de arte completa."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/revistazum.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/11.-TMI-WHITA-49879.png?resize=1024%2C724&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Como de costume, de Alberta Whittle, 2018. Cortesia da artista e do Modern Institute/ Toby Webster Ltd., Glasgow", "credit": "ZUM · Instituto Moreira Salles"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ao olhar para os trabalhos que compõem a série, percebemos sobreposições contrastantes, tanto de linguagens diversas (autorretratos, textos, aquarelas, fotografias e imagens retiradas de HDs, livros ou cadernos) quanto de naturezas e temporalidades distintas. Para a artista, o objetivo é “abordar as histórias da exploração e do colonialismo climático, pois, nos diferentes processos e momentos que se intercalam – entre gerações e tecnologias, com maior atenção à erradicação das tecnologias indígenas –, ainda persiste a sensação de que isso é progresso. É esse atrito entre o progresso – ou o suposto progresso – e as tecnologias negras e indígenas que realmente me incomoda, porque sinto que o conhecimento que nos foi transmitido é frequentemente menosprezado e ignorado.” O resultado formal dessa escavação são composições ao mesmo tempo vibrantes e provocantes, nas quais Whittle toma a liberdade de justapor galáxias e espectros de navios dos séculos 16 e 17, foguetes e insetos, o logo do Google e orquídeas. Passado, presente e futuro são apresentados num mesmo plano."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A coexistência de diferentes estágios desse “suposto progresso” remete diretamente ao conceito do antropólogo mexicano e argentino Néstor García Canclini – postulado no final dos anos 1990 e ainda atual – de multitemporalidade heterogênea , “consequência de uma história na qual a modernização operou poucas vezes mediante a substituição do tradicional e do antigo”. article_text:
Nascida em 1980 na ilha caribenha de Barbados, Alberta Whittle vive e trabalha em Glasgow, na Escócia. Sua prática multifacetada tem como cerne o desenvolvimento de uma resposta pessoal às heranças do tráfico negreiro transatlântico, desmascarando suas conexões com o racismo institucional, a supremacia branca e a emergência climática no presente. Frente a um contexto político opressivo, Whittle busca promover esperança e diferentes formas de resistência, autocuidado e cuidado coletivo. Formada em Belas Artes pelo Edinburgh College of Art, com mestrado pela Glasgow School of Art e doutorado pela University of Edinburgh, atua como Research Associate na University of Johannesburg e já recebeu prêmios como o Paul Hamlyn Foundation Award (2022), o Frieze Artist Award (2020) e o Henry Moore Foundation Artist Award (2020). No começo de 2026, passou uma temporada no Brasil como artista residente do Pivô Salvador, onde se encantou com festividades e rituais coletivos, como a festa de Iemanjá no Rio Vermelho e as atividades da Irmandade da Boa Morte em Cachoeira.

Transitando entre linguagens como vídeo, performance, fotografia, aquarela e bordado, é na técnica da colagem que Alberta Whittle encontra não só seu primeiro refúgio criativo, mas também uma possível chave de leitura do conjunto de sua obra multimídia, que pode ser vista como uma macrocolagem de processos empregados e temas abordados. Na adolescência em Barbados, Alberta sofreu com dores crônicas que a levaram a se mudar, junto à família, para Birmingham, no coração da Inglaterra, em busca de uma cura para a fibromialgia. Antes dessa migração transatlântica de sentido inverso ao dos invasores britânicos que colonizaram a ilha caribenha no século 17, a artista vivia quase em isolamento, relegada à cama na maior parte do tempo. No quarto, seu passatempo preferido era fazer colagens, desenhos e autorretratos – meios predominantes em sua produção até hoje.

Se o porto seguro entre quatro paredes era a assemblagem de imagens coladas sobre papel, lá fora, o que sempre acolheu Alberta foi a profundidade e a vastidão do oceano. Foi isso que a fez escolher, depois de Birmingham, a Escócia como sua nova casa para retomar o contato com as águas, fonte de criatividade e elemento estético e simbólico que permeia toda sua obra. As ondas oceânicas também lambiam o lar temporário que estabeleceu, entre 2012 e 2019, na África do Sul – lugar que a levou a refletir sobre a condição compartilhada de negritude no mundo. Foi em um período de trânsito entre Barbados, Joanesburgo e Cidade do Cabo que Alberta retomou a prática-refúgio da adolescência.

Iniciada em 2016, a série de colagens digitais Business as usual ( Como de costume ) encapsula muitas das questões formais, simbólicas e biográficas de Alberta Whittle, mulher negra, queer , caribenha e escocesa. A forte carga imagética do meio se presta a fomentar discussões sobre migração, pertencimento e direitos da população negra, não apenas no Reino Unido, marcado em 2018 pelo desmonte dos direitos da Geração Windrush [1], mas também em todo o mundo pós-colonial. “O trânsito entre Barbados e Escócia foi muito importante para eu começar a desconstruir como entendemos a história, o território e as pessoas, e de que forma contar as estórias de onde viemos, dentro de nossa história compartilhada”. Por isso, muitas das imagens se situam em espaços limiares entre partida e chegada que, por sua vez, se tornam pano de fundo para invasões ou boas-vindas, encontros ou despedidas, ou tudo ao mesmo tempo. Para Alberta, a colagem permite justamente reunir diferentes ideias, ao passo que mostra suas fissuras e de onde elas vêm, quase como se revelasse suas raízes mais profundas.

O título Business as usual pega emprestada uma expressão idiomática da língua inglesa, que pode ser traduzida livremente para o português como “vida que segue” ou “como de costume”. Para a artista, a frase descreve uma situação contínua e imutável, apesar das dificuldades ou perturbações ao redor. Com uma boa dose de sarcasmo, Alberta se reapropria da fala apaziguadora para endereçar a maneira como o status quo se mantém inalterado, como se nada fosse, ainda que carregado de consequências brutais das histórias colonialistas e imperialistas e dos genocídios ainda em curso. Ao falar sobre essas histórias “difíceis” por meio de suas colagens, a artista busca promover o reconhecimento desse passado ainda tão presente e sua cura. Por isso, ainda que a maior parte das obras da série se situe entre 2016 e 2018, Alberta reforça que esse é um trabalho ainda em curso, pois, assim como em suas performances ou obras coletivas, ele só se conclui a partir da colaboração com o outro; mais especificamente, são as conversas que a série desperta que a tornam uma obra de arte completa.

Ao olhar para os trabalhos que compõem a série, percebemos sobreposições contrastantes, tanto de linguagens diversas (autorretratos, textos, aquarelas, fotografias e imagens retiradas de HDs, livros ou cadernos) quanto de naturezas e temporalidades distintas. Para a artista, o objetivo é “abordar as histórias da exploração e do colonialismo climático, pois, nos diferentes processos e momentos que se intercalam – entre gerações e tecnologias, com maior atenção à erradicação das tecnologias indígenas –, ainda persiste a sensação de que isso é progresso. É esse atrito entre o progresso – ou o suposto progresso – e as tecnologias negras e indígenas que realmente me incomoda, porque sinto que o conhecimento que nos foi transmitido é frequentemente menosprezado e ignorado.” O resultado formal dessa escavação são composições ao mesmo tempo vibrantes e provocantes, nas quais Whittle toma a liberdade de justapor galáxias e espectros de navios dos séculos 16 e 17, foguetes e insetos, o logo do Google e orquídeas. Passado, presente e futuro são apresentados num mesmo plano.

A coexistência de diferentes estágios desse “suposto progresso” remete diretamente ao conceito do antropólogo mexicano e argentino Néstor García Canclini – postulado no final dos anos 1990 e ainda atual – de multitemporalidade heterogênea , “consequência de uma história na qual a modernização operou poucas vezes mediante a substituição do tradicional e do antigo”. Segundo Canclini, a América Latina – “onde as tradições ainda não se foram e a modernidade ainda não terminou de chegar” – é caracterizada pela coexistência de diferentes planos temporais, sendo resultado “da sedimentação, justaposição e entrecruzamento de tradições indígenas […], do hispanismo colonial católico e das ações políticas educativas e comunicacionais modernas” [2]. Mesmo que o território caribenho tenha suas especificidades, ele compartilha das contradições que marcam a América Latina analisada por Canclini, especialmente no que diz respeito à sua condição pós-colonial com consequências ainda vigentes.

Alberta Whittle já identificava essas complexas sobreposições de camadas nas histórias que a mãe da artista – que não sabia nadar, mas sempre a levava à praia – contava sobre o oceano: “Ela me fez parar para pensar que, enquanto contemplamos essas belas águas turquesas da ilha de Barbados, também há navios negreiros enterrados ali embaixo. Há os restos mortais de pessoas escravizadas que foram jogadas ao mar para servir de alimento aos tubarões. Eu sou uma pessoa sensível, por isso, às vezes eu olhava para o oceano e quase sentia como se pudesse ver esses navios chegando”, relembra. Se o presente ainda é assombrado pelo passado, também é possível curar o passado com ações do presente, como evocado no provérbio iorubá “Exu matou um pássaro ontem com uma pedra que jogou hoje”. Se o pássaro é a herança do tráfico negreiro, as colagens de Alberta são a pedra.

Olhos abertos, conchas do mar, frutas tropicais e as águas do oceano são alguns dos elementos recorrentes que irrompem em diversas colagens da série. A vasta iconografia de Alberta Whittle é reunida a partir de um estado de urgência canalizado em um processo criativo ritualístico, intuitivo e corporal: “Eu uso muito o ritual em minha vida e prática. Incenso queimando, velas acesas… São momentos de reflexão e de cura do meu corpo e da minha alma, em que penso nos meus ancestrais e em como prestar tributo ou pedir orientação a eles. Nesse contexto, minhas obras se tornam um feitiço e uma oferenda para ver o que é possível imaginar juntos”, revela. Assim, cada ingrediente que compõe essa oferenda é rico em carga simbólica, além de estética. Os olhos recortados, por exemplo, carregam a dupla consciência de olhar e ser olhado, ações que podem ter conotações contraditórias, segundo a perspectiva. Do ponto de vista gráfico, a repetição desses órgãos confere um “glitch”, um ruído na composição – recurso presente não só nas colagens, mas também nos filmes de Alberta, que não gosta de superfícies achatadas, e sim de brincar com texturas e criar padronagens a partir delas.

As conchas também são um elemento gráfico e simbólico ambivalente, podendo ser utilizadas como adorno (a mãe de Alberta sempre as empregou para produzir joias) ou como ferramenta em rituais religiosos, enquanto mantêm uma ligação direta à história da escravidão, na qual foram moeda de troca para a compra e venda de almas. Alberta se interessa por essas múltiplas camadas de interpretação que habitam o objeto e pelo atrito que elas produzem. Além disso, ao lado dos olhos, as conchas também demonstram o interesse sensorial da artista que, a depender da disposição da imagem, pode transformar um búzio em ouvido que escuta ou em boca que fala.

Até mesmo o corpo da artista está sujeito a contradições e, por isso, também se configura como dispositivo recorrente na série. Enquanto mulher negra caribenha e escocesa de pele clara, Alberta Whittle põe seu corpo fotografado em jogo para as inúmeras leituras que ele suscita nas diferentes comunidades que contribuem para a formação de sua identidade. Enquanto nas ruas da Cidade do Cabo as pessoas paravam para perguntar à artista se ela era alemã, por outro lado, no Reino Unido ser ao mesmo tempo negra e escocesa é visto como uma impossibilidade. Assim, a inserção de sua própria imagem, para Alberta, é uma forma de refletir sobre miscigenação cultural e sobre como é possível pertencer a mais de uma identidade ao mesmo tempo.

Alberta empresta seu corpo para a reencenação de mitos e arquétipos presentes em Business as usual . Em algumas colagens, é possível reconhecer a pose altiva da Estátua da Liberdade, símbolo de independência, democracia e esperança, valores pouco em sintonia com o atual governo dos Estados Unidos – contradição verbalizada no título (UN)welcome (2018) (um jogo de palavras entre a sigla das Nações Unidas em inglês, “UN”, que também funciona como negação da palavra “welcome”, bem-vindos). Já em C.R.E.A.M. (2017), as madeixas da artista assumem a forma de um ninho de cobras – uma alusão direta ao mito grego da Medusa, uma criatura monstruosa com serpentes no lugar dos cabelos e um olhar que petrificava quem ousasse encará-la. “Sempre fui fascinada por esses arquétipos femininos e pela maneira como moldam a forma como as mulheres são vistas e tratadas no mundo. Para mim, a Medusa é um símbolo tão potente quanto incompreendido. Mas, ao mesmo tempo que exploro o poder desse mito, quero representá-lo do meu jeito”, afirma Alberta, que adiciona à figura mitológica uma pitada de “sazon” caribenho, como a pose agachada típica da cultura dancehall anos 90, cocos e bananas, além de moedas, notas e correntes de ouro. “Trago minhas próprias perspectivas para me compreender dentro desses arquétipos, refletindo sobre o que me é útil para falar sobre o conflito entre extração, indigenismo, negritude e feminilidade”, completa.

A palavra escrita é mais um elemento que agrega a diversas colagens da série. Para Alberta, o texto é um recurso que, apesar de tirá-la de sua zona de conforto para uma experimentação poética, a aproxima do público, criando uma ponte para que sua narrativa chegue ao espectador com força em tempos de atenção dividida e interpretações equivocadas. Muitas das frases – assim como o título não só da série, mas também de cada uma das obras – têm um tom ao mesmo tempo irônico e político. Entre elas, uma brincadeira com o alfabeto guia a leitura das obras, a exemplo de C is for colonial fantasy (“C de fantasia colonial”) ou I is for the Illusion of Inclusion (“I de Ilusão de Inclusão”). Em outros casos, elas funcionam como reza ou feitiço: I wrap myself in rainbows / protection from your gaze (“me envolvo em arco-íris / proteção do teu olhar”). De maneira jocosa ou ritualística, as palavras levam diretamente ao cerne de temas urgentes problematizados pela artista. Imagem e texto se complementam e potencializam.

Por meio da junção inusitada de elementos iconográficos, palavras e sua própria imagem, Alberta Whittle busca evocar uma nova ideia de futuro, de como estar no mundo, distante do extrativismo, do capitalismo e das desigualdades que provocam. O caminho para construir essa futuridade de cuidado encontra-se na retomada dos rituais herdados pela população negra, pelas mulheres negras, pelas “mulheres de maioria global”, nas palavras da artista. Nesse sentido, as colagens, enquanto oferendas, são portais que convidam a desacelerar e a parar para escutar os ancestrais – que podem vir do passado, do presente ou até mesmo do futuro – e aprender com eles (ou, melhor, elas) a promover cura e esperança.

“Para mim, arte é uma prática de esperança. Contra o entorpecimento generalizado diante de tantas notícias ruins, eu prefiro manter a energia circulando. Mesmo que muitas das minhas obras surjam de um lugar de dor, frustração, raiva e tristeza, nessa troca de conversas, de honestidade e vulnerabilidade, a esperança é renovada e compartilhada. Não podemos permanecer estagnados. Mantendo as coisas em movimento, esses trabalhos são feitiços de esperança.” Com essa série, Alberta Whittle grita aos sussurros que não dá mais para continuar business as usual , seguir a vida como de costume. Por meio do encanto e da reflexão provocados pela arte, é possível imaginar e construir outros futuros. Axé! ///

Marina Dias Teixeira é editora, curadora e jornalista cultural baseada em São Paulo e formada em Estudos de Mídia e Cultura pela Universidade de Artes de Londres. Com especial interesse em arte afro-diaspórica e latino-americana, editou cerca de 20 livros, entre eles Pinacoteca de São Paulo 120 Anos e Máquina de Ritmo: Som e Música na Arte Brasileira , do qual também foi organizadora. Colabora com veículos de arte, design e arquitetura, além de desenvolver projetos curatoriais próprios, como a exposição Fio Condutor , realizada em 2026.

article_text:
Le Premi Fotografia Femenina Fisheye x InCadaqués 2026 a récompensé Julie Peiffer pour Renversement , une série où la nature fragile croise quelques portraits. Cette dernière est à découvrir pendant cette dixième édition du festival espagnol, qui s’achèvera le 25 octobre prochain.

Le festival InCadaqués a lancé sa dixième édition en Catalogne, en Espagne. Jusqu’au 25 octobre 2026, le public peut y découvrir 25 expositions portées par 40 photographes venus du monde entier. Parmi eux se trouve notamment Julie Peiffer, lauréate du Premi Fotografia Femenina 2026, un prix en partenariat avec Fisheye qui célèbre le regard féminin au sein du 8e art. Au fil de projets marqués par le temps long, l’artiste française sonde les liens qui unissent le corps, la mémoire et le territoire. Elle porte un intérêt particulier à ce qui ne se voit pas forcément, mais laisse une empreinte pérenne.

Saisir des déséquilibres discrets

« Un matin, le chant d’un oiseau m’a semblé un cri, explique Julie Peiffer en introduction à sa série . Ce désordre a bouleversé ma manière de percevoir notre milieu : sa lumière, sa densité, sa vibration, la promesse même des saisons. Enfant, je croyais que mon père pouvait arrêter le vent ; cette croyance disait la confiance absolue que j’avais dans la permanence du monde. Aujourd’hui, je vois les chaleurs écraser nos étés, les forêts se taire, la pluie ronger nos repères ; le monde m’apparaît traversé par une matière invisible. Mes photographies cherchent à en révéler la trace, dans l’épaisseur même de l’image. » Face aux métamorphoses constantes du territoire, l’artiste utilise son médium pour saisir des déséquilibres encore discrets. Pour les matérialiser, elle inverse le sens des tirages, les transforme en négatifs et les retravaille jusqu’à faire émerger « une matière instable, vulnérable » . « Renversement ne propose ni constat ni réponse. C’est un espace de coexistence fragile. Un lieu où le paysage n’est plus regardé, mais éprouvé » , conclut-elle.

Intime

Partenaire

article_text:
In the street, two silhouettes advance, wearing studded belts, sunglasses, leather biker jackets and torn tights. Further on, a couple kiss, their mohawks and tattoos matching. In Dave Clarke’s photographs, on show until the end of September at Jardin21 in Paris, the compositions are raw, the monochromes contrasted, the grain powerful. Nicknamed “The Baron of Techno”, the DJ, producer and remixer has worked with Depeche Mode, The Chemical Brothers and Placebo. He first tried photography in his youth, borrowing his father’s old camera. “But film was expensive, and developing it even more so. So I spent my pocket money on 45s and tapes instead, because you could always ‘develop’ those live, without waiting for a result, or record over them if you got it wrong,” he continues.

An emblematic figure of the techno scene, he draws inspiration from “gothic atmospheres, monochrome punk, soundscapes”, travels to many cities and gladly gets lost on foot. These experiences once again lead Clarke toward visual experimentation, a new way of translating the emotions he feels through sound. But how do the two media feed each other? How do scene photographers manage to impose their aesthetic, their own writing, when they capture the essence of an artist whose work already exists? Passionate about music, Jessica Attia and David Fitt have, like Dave Clarke, made the music scene their favorite space of expression. In the whirl of concerts and festivals, in the studio right beside the performers, or simply around a street corner, they turn composers and their fans into their preferred subjects. They capture an atmosphere, a sensibility, while preserving their singularity. It is a balancing act they have learned to master.

Forging Bonds

“I see my music and my photography as art forms that come together and symbolize my interpretation of the world, my need to try to understand it. I would say music makes me want to shoot, and shooting lets me empty my hyperactive mind. It’s a kind of zen,” Dave Clarke explains. The link between the two media seems obvious to him: “Eyes and ears are connected to the brain, so trying to separate their creative processes almost seems like an oxymoron,” he admits.

For Jessica Attia too, music is a binding thread, a necessary source of inspiration for her visual research. “It is constantly present in my mind and always finds a place in my images,” she confides. A devotee of Polaroid and analog film, the young photographer has already had the biggest names of the scene in front of her lens, among them Billie Eilish, Post Malone and DJ Snake. Their universes differ, yet she approaches every encounter the same way: fully immersed. “I think there is a part of truth, a part of themselves in their music, even if it isn’t the whole of who they are. That is why, as an artist, I have to listen to everything, feel their compositions, understand their creation,” she continues.

It was by “hanging around concerts all the time” that David Fitt made a place for himself in the rock and metal scene. “When I started getting interested in it, a photographer lent me his second camera body so I could experiment. I gave the images to the bands and, little by little, I became known,” he recalls. He often initiates the meetings with the artists he photographs, and considers himself lucky: “I work 90% of the time with people whose music I love,” he says. It is a starting point that allows him to build ties with those he admires. “I feel very privileged to be a collaborator, a fan and a friend to them all at once,” he admits. For him, such prior knowledge is essential: when you are already steeped in an artist’s compositions, it becomes easy to summon them through images.

Letting an Identity Emerge

But how, as a photographer, do you resist the urge to disappear? How do you reconcile two artistic representations? For Jessica Attia, everything comes down to connection: “I want to draw them somewhere they don’t expect to go. That’s where my own vision can take over. If I fully respect their identity, my emotional filter kicks in once we’re in the same room. It’s a kind of sharing: their world and their energy through my prism,” she explains.

David Fitt, for his part, does extensive research, looks at existing visuals, discovers who made them and asks questions to grasp what the band wants. “I also tell myself that if they come to me, it’s so that I make their universe my own,” he admits. He aims to combine the aesthetic of his subjects with his own language. In the end, the pictures fit together like pieces of a puzzle from which a global identity emerges. In Jessica Attia’s work, nearly all the details vanish into the penumbra, chiaroscuros turn abstract, and blurs summon an atmosphere, a mood, rather than a constructed narrative. In David Fitt’s portraits, colored halos set the scene, and enhance or conceal bodies and features. It is a dark, dreamlike universe from which the artists emerge as spectral, almost fantastical figures. “You have to be able to feel the atmosphere visually, or at least the image should show a facet that the music doesn’t give us,” he concludes. “Putting a face to a name makes a project more human, deeper, more compelling, all the more so at a time when AI is sweeping in.”

More information on Dave Clarke , David Fitt and Jessica Attia on their respective websites.

article_text:
写真家・柴田徹之による個展「美しき奇妙な夢見し ― India illusion ―」が、2026年11月26日（木）から12月1日（火）まで、東京・国立のギャラリー国立で開催される。

本展では、ガンジス川をヒマラヤへと遡り、ベンガル湾へと下る旅のなかで撮影された100点以上の写真を展示。冬霧に包まれた聖地を行き交う巡礼者たちの姿と、ヒンドゥー教の放浪修行者「サドゥ」たちの肖像を中心に、インドの宗教的風景に漂う夢と現実の境界を浮かび上がらせる。

柴田が捉えたのは、巡礼の情景に立ち現れる「マーヤ（幻影）」と、そのなかに確かな存在感を放つ修行者たち。写真を壁面に直接貼り付ける自由なレイアウトによって、美しい大地とそこに潜む奇妙な影が交錯する空間をつくり出す。

さらに、デカン高原の密林に眠る知られざる古代壁画の写真も公開。インドの風土と信仰、悠久の時間が重なり合う写真展となる。

タイトル

柴田徹之「美しき奇妙な夢見し ― India illusion ―」

場所

ギャラリー国立（東京都国立市中1-9-18 NTC高橋ビル1F）

会期

2026年11月26日（木）〜12月1日（火）

時間

11:00〜18:00（最終日は16:00まで）

休み

無し

料金

無料

article_text:
A man conceived through sperm donation, unsure of his place in the world, sets out on a journey to Korea in “ The Blue Breaks ,” an adaptation of Machiya Ryohei’s 2016 novel by Japanese filmmaker Uchiyama Takuya (“Numb”). The Japan-Italy co-production was among the projects at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market.

The protagonist, Shukichi, is a rootless part-time worker in his thirties living at Japan’s western edge. His sense of detachment grows when he discovers that his girlfriend, with whom he lives, has a son she no longer has custody of. A night spent with a solitary boxer of Korean descent then throws his sense of identity and sexuality into further confusion.

Related Stories

Netflix, Bengali Streamer Hoichoi Partner to Bring Series to Hindi, Tamil and Telugu Audiences

Netflix Content Chief Bela Bajaria on Overseeing Global Storytelling: 'My Super Power Is I Hire Really Great People and I Let Them Do Their Job'

He later meets Toko, a young woman who is terminally ill but carries herself lightly, smoking and smiling despite the little time she has left. Her outlook gradually leaves its mark on him. Eventually Shukichi and the people around him travel to Korea together, where they reckon with one another’s lives and deaths.

Uchiyama, who has previously written his own screenplays from personal experience, said he felt drawn to the book in part because it was published in the year he started making films, and because Machiya wrote it at the age Uchiyama is now.

“Shukichi, the protagonist, struggles with the part of himself that never quite became ‘manly.’ I’ve also spent much of my life feeling uncomfortable with what society expects a man to be,” Uchiyama said.

He described the characters as people whose lives look very different from one another’s, and said Japan still expects everyone to be alike.

“Diversity isn’t something new. It’s always been there, even if we haven’t always acknowledged it,” Uchiyama said. “I wanted to approach these feelings with a sense of lightness, and to make a film about love that is unapologetically romantic.”

Japanese producer Satoh Naomi of Differentia is behind the project, with Parsifal Reparato of Italian company Antropica as co-producer. The team is working on the screenplay, casting and financing, with a shoot planned for 2027 and completion in 2028, and is targeting a premiere at an international festival.

Satoh said the two connected over a shared sense of not fitting the roles expected of them, whether in society at large or within the film business, and that films that resist categories can be hard to finance in Japan.

“When ‘Numb’ was selected for the Berlinale, it gave me real proof that Takuya’s work could resonate with audiences beyond Japan,” Satoh said.

In Tokyo, the producers made headway on the remaining financing and find international co-production partners, sales agents and distributors who could take the film beyond Japan and Italy.

Reparato said the film’s appeal lies in how it rethinks family and identity, and that Antropica, which has been active in Asia for years, including in Vietnam, sees the project as a way to deepen ties with Japanese cinema, helped by Italy and Japan’s bilateral co-production framework.

“At this historical moment, building bridges is more important than ever,” Reparato said.

Uchiyama has also wrapped shooting on a separate project, which is now moving into editing.

The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market ran as part of TIFFCOM , the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival .

"這些山水畫運用了多種水墨技巧，包括拓印與水拓，營造植物濃密或岩石嶙峋的景象。深沉的灰黑墨色與濃紫、鮮橙、粉紅、紅色及綠色交織，構成一片迷幻的天空，令人彷彿得以窺見一個超凡脫俗的靈性世界。展覽亦播放了一段錄影片段，記錄唐家偉在1992年於香港藝術中心舉行的「天界」展覽開幕時接受訪問的情景。他在片中談及宗教探索，以及山嶽在其靈性世界中的核心地位，並表示自己只有「在佛陀的加持下」才能創作這些畫作。唐家偉留下的文字筆記，部分由姐姐唐慧中從他的工作室和家中整理出來，並在展覽中放大印製，懸掛於畫作旁邊。筆記進一步透露，他希望來世能夠投生於中國佛教觀念中的西方山嶽或西方極樂世界，也就是阿彌陀佛的淨土。他自幼接受基督教教育，在不同信仰之間摸索，逐漸形成一套融合多種宗教元素的個人信仰。", "這種張力猶如一股隨時會在紙上爆發的被壓抑能量，是其作品的常態之一。唐家偉曾向家人表達過他想要接受性別肯定手術並成為女性的願望。雖然他的家人準備好支援他完成這一轉變，但這項手術無法在香港進行，且在當時承受著比今天更大的污名。最終，唐家偉並沒有接受手術，而是將這種被壓縮的生命力傾注於作品之中，賦予它們非凡的強度。展覽中的大型畫作對他而言非常重要，儘管他隨後因所服藥物的身體副作用（影響關節並使他昏昏欲睡）而被迫停止繪製這些作品。", "然而，在他所有的掙扎中，水墨始終是他不離不棄的媒介。「唐家偉對他的藝術工藝有著深厚的奉獻精神，」唐慧中說，「儘管他總是為自己作畫，但他希望做到最好，並不知疲倦地尋找自己的聲音——力求獨一無二。他從不滿足；當他達成一個目標時，他會設定另一個目標。他在生活中經歷了許多掙扎，甚至在自己的藝術中也是如此。我能感受到這些掙扎，正是這種不斷的張力驅動著他的藝術。他非常聰明、安靜且性格溫和，但由於他的心理健康狀況，他也有黑暗的一面。這對他來說不容易——對我們家人來說也是如此。」", "亞洲協會為唐家偉舉辦回顧展「筆歌墨舞：唐家偉的藝術」，讓公眾有機會欣賞這位鮮為人知的藝術家多姿多彩、一貫高水平的繪畫作品。唐家偉1957年生於香港，17歲開始學習水墨畫，此後一生不斷探索這種媒介的可能性，期間亦曾在香港及多倫多求學。他的創作從以中國傳統繪畫大師為靈感的學院派作品，逐漸轉向與水墨的接觸及其可能性。晚年時，他創作了一系列完全不使用畫筆的作品，以手指、指甲和雙手作畫，令水墨成為一種具有觸感、近乎雕塑般的媒介。雖然這種徒手作畫的方式相當新穎，但在水墨藝術中亦有先例，例如清代畫家高其佩（1660-1734），唐家偉很可能認識其作品。", Heaven」展覽開幕式上錄製的，唐家偉在其中談到了他的宗教探索以及山脈在他的靈性形式中扮演的核心地位，並補充說他只有「在佛陀的加持下」才能創作這些畫作。在他留下的書面筆記中，這些筆記由他的姐姐唐慧中從他的工作室和家中收集並提供，其中一些已被複製、放大並懸掛在本次展覽畫作旁邊的牆上，他進一步表達了他在中國佛教西方山或西方淨土（阿彌陀佛淨土的變體）概念中重生的願望，儘管他的基督教背景意味著他似乎經常在融合了不同信仰元素的個人宗教形式中前行。", article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "The retrospective at the Asia Society of Wesley Tongson’s work, Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink, has offered the public the possibility of seeing some of this too-little-known artist’s impressively varied and consistently high-quality paintings. Born in Hong Kong in 1957, Tongson began studying ink when he was 17 and kept developing his approach to the medium throughout his life, while pursuing his studies in Hong Kong and Toronto. He went from more academic pieces, often inspired by masters from the Chinese canon, to a much more tactile and physical relationship with ink and its possibilities. He produced, in his later years, paintings made entirely without a brush, instead using his own fingers, nails and hands – turning ink into a tactile, nearly sculptural element. While his approach to hand-painting was pretty unconventional, there are precedents in ink art, like the Qing dynasty painter Gao Qipei (1660-1734), who was likely known to Tongson."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The show is curated by Julia M White and Yi Yi Mon (Rosaline) Kyo, with crucial input from Tongson’s sister, Cynthia Tongson. “I am involved in the show as a supporter to the two curators,” she says. “They were the ones who wanted to do a Tongson exhibition and insisted on doing it in Hong Kong, as they felt Wesley was still overlooked in his hometown.” She shared his archives and personal notes, and allowed them to interview his former classmates, friends, family members and collectors."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NZ8_3677.jpg?resize=840%2C560&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Exhibition view of Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink by Wesley Tongson at Asia Society Hong Kong Center. Courtesy Asia Society Hong Kong Center. Photo: Felix SC Wong.", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Divided into five different sections, the exhibition brings together pieces scattered among museums and private collections to offer a more complete view of a body of work that is both vast in scope and stubbornly dedicated to all the possibilities of ink. The first room presents studies of rocks, plants and water that evolve from the classical – like the undated Untitled (Orchids) ,which offers a formal but still forceful and lively composition of orchids on rocks – to works like Untitled (Orchid and Rock) , dated 2010, two years before his death, which appears as a burst of ink on paper, a dynamic, passionate take on the same theme, produced using his fingers and nails."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Diagnosed with schizophrenia at 15 and put on psychiatric medication, Tongson struggled with mental illness and gender identity throughout his life, and used his artistic practice to explore and tame the difficulties he faced. Spiritual Mountains , for example, his last series, produced from 2009 to 2012, consists of very large paintings on which he created the shapes of misty mountains through finger painting and splashed ink, made dreamier yet by the addition of colour. He put on the canvas his spiritual pursuits, as he tried to overcome anxiety and find solace in exploring a number of spiritual and religious traditions, from Buddhism and Daoism to Christianity."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NZ8_3786-%E7%B7%A8%E8%BC%AF-1.jpg?resize=840%2C546&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Exhibition view of Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink by Wesley Tongson at Asia Society Hong Kong Center. Courtesy Asia Society Hong Kong Center. Photo: Felix SC Wong.", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These mountain landscapes are produced using different ink techniques, from rubbing to marbling, to create the effect of dense vegetation or jagged rocks. The deep grey-black of the ink is set against deep purples, bright oranges, pinks, red and greens that form a lysergic sky, underlining the possibility of watching a spiritual, otherworldly landscape. In a video interview that can be viewed at the show, recorded at the opening of his 1992 Mountains of Heaven show at the Hong Kong Arts Centre, Tongson talks about his religious explorations and the central role that mountains play in his form of spirituality, adding that he could only create these paintings “with the Buddha’s blessing”. In the written notes that he left behind, collected from his studio and his home and provided by his sister Cynthia Tongson, some of which have been reproduced, enlarged and hung on the walls next to the paintings for this exhibition, he further expresses his wish to be reborn in the Chinese Buddhist idea of a western mountain or western paradise, variants of Pure Land Buddhism’s land of the Amitabha Buddha, even if his Christian upbringing meant that he often seemed to move in a personal form of religion that mixed elements from different faiths."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Palace of Royal Purple (1994), the ink is first splashed onto the board, then made to form rivulets by turning the board around to create different directions for it to drip, producing a pattern reminiscent of trees and vegetation. A later Untitled (landscape) from 2002 uses the same technique for the small patches of black ink, which are overpowered by the emerald green of the mountains and a bright yellow and pink that float in the valley in front of them, under a bright yellow sky filled with clouds and stars."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These mystical, hazy mountains, while coalescing into a full-blown series in his later years, are a presence throughout his productive years, as can be seen in Landscape 2 (1987), in black, dark pink and greenish blue on gold paper, with an inscription that reads “Green mountains and red clouds rise with a tranquil morning, a record from the elegant peaks studio, Tang Jiawei (Tongson’s name in Mandarin) with new ideas of splashed ink, I thought such fleeting visions must be preserved” (translation by Keyu Yan, from the exhibition catalogue). The seal with which he marked the painting reads: Long live Jiawei."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The spiritual practices he pursued, of which he wrote quite frequently in his notes, tended to clash with his gender ambiguity: he sometimes wrote about his desire to get married – which he wrote with the Chinese character that implies a woman getting married to a man, jia – and how this was in contradiction with his Chan (Zen) Buddhist practice. Occasionally, he would sign some of his paintings, like the Untitiled (Bamboo) of 2012, a reproduction of a group of bamboo branches with thick foliage, which he signed Painted by Shandou (meaning “mountain Daoist”). The piece, produced through finger painting, seems to portray a profound inner tension, tamed by the edges of the paper: the upper part of the dark bamboo leaves and branches are cut as if seen through a window, or as if the limited surface of the paper could not contain all their vitality and emotion."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/NZ8_4156.jpg?resize=840%2C560&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Exhibition view of Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink by Wesley Tongson at Asia Society Hong Kong Center. Courtesy Asia Society Hong Kong Center. Photo: Felix SC Wong.", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Also worthy of attention are his calligraphic works, which once more span the whole range from classical compositions that pay homage to Chinese masters to exuberant, highly expressive pieces produced mostly with fingers, hands and nails. The latter stretch the Chinese characters represented on the paper into abstract form, capable of conveying anxiety, hardship and an interior force with which Tongson constantly battled. In the piece With the Prevalence of Ink, We Can Observe the Teachings of Buddha, Whose Wisdom is All-encompassing, painted in 2011 and signed Shandou, the energy of the Chinese characters is achieved by first dripping the ink on the white paper, then producing each individual word with his nails and fingers, creating multi-stroke characters that merge abstraction with writing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This tension, like a suppressed energy that would burst out on the paper, is one of the constants of his works. Tongson expressed to his family his desire to undergo gender-affirming surgery and become a woman. And while his family was ready to support him through that transition, the operation could not be done in Hong Kong and carried an even greater stigma at the time than it does today. In the end, Tongson did not undergo the surgery and kept pouring this compressed vitality into his works, giving them an extraordinary strength. The large-scale paintings in the exhibition were very important to him, even if he was then forced to stop painting them due to the physical side-effects of the medications he was on, which affected his joints and made him drowsy."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And yet, throughout his struggles, ink was always what he stayed with. “Wesley was deeply devoted to his craft,” says Cynthia Tongson. “Even though he always painted for himself, he wanted to do his best and worked relentlessly to find his own voice – to be unique. He was never satisfied; when he reached one goal, he would set another goal. He had many struggles in life, even with his own art. I feel these struggles, the constant tension that drove his art. He was very smart, quiet and mild in nature but he had a dark side due to his mental health condition. "他經常在筆記中記錄自己追尋的靈性修行，而這些追求往往與他對自身性別的模糊認同產生衝突。他有時會寫下自己希望結婚的念頭，並使用中文字「嫁」來表達，同時又提到這個願望與他的禪宗佛教修行矛盾。他偶爾也會以別號為作品署名，例如2012年的《無題（竹）》，描繪一組枝葉茂密的竹枝，署名為「山斗」（意為「山中道士」）。這幅手指創作的作品似乎呈現出深刻的內在張力，卻又被紙張的邊界所約束。畫面上方深色的竹葉與枝幹被截斷，彷彿是透過窗戶向外觀看，又或者是紙張有限的表面根本無法容納竹枝所蘊含的生命力與情感。"}, article_text:
The retrospective at the Asia Society of Wesley Tongson’s work, Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink, has offered the public the possibility of seeing some of this too-little-known artist’s impressively varied and consistently high-quality paintings. Born in Hong Kong in 1957, Tongson began studying ink when he was 17 and kept developing his approach to the medium throughout his life, while pursuing his studies in Hong Kong and Toronto. He went from more academic pieces, often inspired by masters from the Chinese canon, to a much more tactile and physical relationship with ink and its possibilities. He produced, in his later years, paintings made entirely without a brush, instead using his own fingers, nails and hands – turning ink into a tactile, nearly sculptural element. While his approach to hand-painting was pretty unconventional, there are precedents in ink art, like the Qing dynasty painter Gao Qipei (1660-1734), who was likely known to Tongson.

The show is curated by Julia M White and Yi Yi Mon (Rosaline) Kyo, with crucial input from Tongson’s sister, Cynthia Tongson. “I am involved in the show as a supporter to the two curators,” she says. “They were the ones who wanted to do a Tongson exhibition and insisted on doing it in Hong Kong, as they felt Wesley was still overlooked in his hometown.” She shared his archives and personal notes, and allowed them to interview his former classmates, friends, family members and collectors.

Divided into five different sections, the exhibition brings together pieces scattered among museums and private collections to offer a more complete view of a body of work that is both vast in scope and stubbornly dedicated to all the possibilities of ink. The first room presents studies of rocks, plants and water that evolve from the classical – like the undated Untitled (Orchids) ,which offers a formal but still forceful and lively composition of orchids on rocks – to works like Untitled (Orchid and Rock) , dated 2010, two years before his death, which appears as a burst of ink on paper, a dynamic, passionate take on the same theme, produced using his fingers and nails.

Diagnosed with schizophrenia at 15 and put on psychiatric medication, Tongson struggled with mental illness and gender identity throughout his life, and used his artistic practice to explore and tame the difficulties he faced. Spiritual Mountains , for example, his last series, produced from 2009 to 2012, consists of very large paintings on which he created the shapes of misty mountains through finger painting and splashed ink, made dreamier yet by the addition of colour. He put on the canvas his spiritual pursuits, as he tried to overcome anxiety and find solace in exploring a number of spiritual and religious traditions, from Buddhism and Daoism to Christianity.

These mountain landscapes are produced using different ink techniques, from rubbing to marbling, to create the effect of dense vegetation or jagged rocks. The deep grey-black of the ink is set against deep purples, bright oranges, pinks, red and greens that form a lysergic sky, underlining the possibility of watching a spiritual, otherworldly landscape. In a video interview that can be viewed at the show, recorded at the opening of his 1992 Mountains of Heaven show at the Hong Kong Arts Centre, Tongson talks about his religious explorations and the central role that mountains play in his form of spirituality, adding that he could only create these paintings “with the Buddha’s blessing”. In the written notes that he left behind, collected from his studio and his home and provided by his sister Cynthia Tongson, some of which have been reproduced, enlarged and hung on the walls next to the paintings for this exhibition, he further expresses his wish to be reborn in the Chinese Buddhist idea of a western mountain or western paradise, variants of Pure Land Buddhism’s land of the Amitabha Buddha, even if his Christian upbringing meant that he often seemed to move in a personal form of religion that mixed elements from different faiths.

In Palace of Royal Purple (1994), the ink is first splashed onto the board, then made to form rivulets by turning the board around to create different directions for it to drip, producing a pattern reminiscent of trees and vegetation. A later Untitled (landscape) from 2002 uses the same technique for the small patches of black ink, which are overpowered by the emerald green of the mountains and a bright yellow and pink that float in the valley in front of them, under a bright yellow sky filled with clouds and stars.

These mystical, hazy mountains, while coalescing into a full-blown series in his later years, are a presence throughout his productive years, as can be seen in Landscape 2 (1987), in black, dark pink and greenish blue on gold paper, with an inscription that reads “Green mountains and red clouds rise with a tranquil morning, a record from the elegant peaks studio, Tang Jiawei (Tongson’s name in Mandarin) with new ideas of splashed ink, I thought such fleeting visions must be preserved” (translation by Keyu Yan, from the exhibition catalogue). The seal with which he marked the painting reads: Long live Jiawei.

The spiritual practices he pursued, of which he wrote quite frequently in his notes, tended to clash with his gender ambiguity: he sometimes wrote about his desire to get married – which he wrote with the Chinese character that implies a woman getting married to a man, jia – and how this was in contradiction with his Chan (Zen) Buddhist practice. Occasionally, he would sign some of his paintings, like the Untitiled (Bamboo) of 2012, a reproduction of a group of bamboo branches with thick foliage, which he signed Painted by Shandou (meaning “mountain Daoist”). The piece, produced through finger painting, seems to portray a profound inner tension, tamed by the edges of the paper: the upper part of the dark bamboo leaves and branches are cut as if seen through a window, or as if the limited surface of the paper could not contain all their vitality and emotion.

Also worthy of attention are his calligraphic works, which once more span the whole range from classical compositions that pay homage to Chinese masters to exuberant, highly expressive pieces produced mostly with fingers, hands and nails. The latter stretch the Chinese characters represented on the paper into abstract form, capable of conveying anxiety, hardship and an interior force with which Tongson constantly battled. In the piece With the Prevalence of Ink, We Can Observe the Teachings of Buddha, Whose Wisdom is All-encompassing, painted in 2011 and signed Shandou, the energy of the Chinese characters is achieved by first dripping the ink on the white paper, then producing each individual word with his nails and fingers, creating multi-stroke characters that merge abstraction with writing.

This tension, like a suppressed energy that would burst out on the paper, is one of the constants of his works. Tongson expressed to his family his desire to undergo gender-affirming surgery and become a woman. And while his family was ready to support him through that transition, the operation could not be done in Hong Kong and carried an even greater stigma at the time than it does today. In the end, Tongson did not undergo the surgery and kept pouring this compressed vitality into his works, giving them an extraordinary strength. The large-scale paintings in the exhibition were very important to him, even if he was then forced to stop painting them due to the physical side-effects of the medications he was on, which affected his joints and made him drowsy.

And yet, throughout his struggles, ink was always what he stayed with. “Wesley was deeply devoted to his craft,” says Cynthia Tongson. “Even though he always painted for himself, he wanted to do his best and worked relentlessly to find his own voice – to be unique. He was never satisfied; when he reached one goal, he would set another goal. He had many struggles in life, even with his own art. I feel these struggles, the constant tension that drove his art. He was very smart, quiet and mild in nature but he had a dark side due to his mental health condition. It was not easy for him – nor for us, his family.”

The Asia Society’s show brings back into Hong Kong’s art scene a highly original, uniquely forceful painter, whose works are testimony to an incredibly complex biography.

在《Palace of Royal Purple》（1994年）中，唐家偉先在畫板上潑墨，再透過轉動畫板改變墨汁流淌的方向，形成一道道墨痕，構成令人聯想起樹木與植被的圖案。2002年創作的另一幅《無題（山水）》，同樣運用這種技法處理畫面中一小片黑色墨跡，不過被山巒中濃烈的翠綠色，以及漂浮於前方山谷的鮮黃色與粉紅色所壓過。上方則是一片明亮的黃色天空，佈滿雲朵與星辰。

這些神秘而朦朧的山巒，雖然在他晚年才發展成完整系列，卻一直貫穿他多年的創作生涯，《山水2》（1987年）便是一例。作品以黑色、深粉紅及藍綠色繪於金色紙上，並附有題款：「青山紅霞晨昇平，蒼雅秀峰堂紀，唐家偉潑墨新意，浮之應當記也」（摘自展覽圖錄，英文版由嚴柯煜翻譯）。畫作上的印識則刻有「家偉長壽」。

他經常在筆記中記錄自己追尋的靈性修行，而這些追求往往與他對自身性別的模糊認同產生衝突。他有時會寫下自己希望結婚的念頭，並使用中文字「嫁」來表達，同時又提到這個願望與他的禪宗佛教修行矛盾。他偶爾也會以別號為作品署名，例如2012年的《無題（竹）》，描繪一組枝葉茂密的竹枝，署名為「山斗」（意為「山中道士」）。這幅手指創作的作品似乎呈現出深刻的內在張力，卻又被紙張的邊界所約束。畫面上方深色的竹葉與枝幹被截斷，彷彿是透過窗戶向外觀看，又或者是紙張有限的表面根本無法容納竹枝所蘊含的生命力與情感。

他的書法作品同樣值得細看，涵蓋了向中國傳統大師致敬的古典構圖，以及主要以手指、雙手和指甲創作、充滿奔放表現力的作品。後者將紙上的中文字拉伸、變形，推向抽象的形態，藉此傳達焦慮、困境，以及唐家偉一生不斷抗衡的內在力量。2011年創作、署名「山斗」的作品《墨道揚，縱驕碍，憶佛始中求，佛智因無漏也》，便展現了中文字的力量。唐家偉先讓墨汁滴落在白紙上，再以指甲和手指逐一寫出每個字，形成筆畫層層交疊的漢字，令抽象藝術與文字書寫融為一體。

這種張力是他作品中反覆出現的特質，猶如一種被壓抑的能量隨時可能在紙上爆發。唐家偉曾向家人表達，希望接受性別肯定手術成為女性。雖然家人表示支持他完成這個轉變，但當時香港無法進行這類手術，而負面標籤比今天更為嚴重。所以最後他並沒有接受手術，而是持續將這股被壓抑的生命力注入作品之中，賦予畫作非凡的力量。展覽中的大型畫作對唐家偉而言尤其重要。然而，由於他服用的藥物帶來身體副作用，影響關節並令他昏昏欲睡，他最終被迫停止創作這類作品。

儘管一生歷經種種掙扎，水墨始終是唐家偉堅持的創作媒介。姐姐唐慧中說：「家偉深深投入自己的藝術創作。雖然他一直只是為自己而畫，但他總是希望做到最好，不斷尋找屬於自己的聲音，力求獨一無二。他從不安於現狀，達成一個目標後，便會為自己訂立下一個目標。他一生面對許多掙扎，甚至包括與自己的藝術創作之間的拉扯。我能感受到這些掙扎，以及那股持續推動他創作的張力。他非常聰明，性格安靜溫和，但受精神健康狀況影響，他亦有陰暗的一面。這對他而言並不容易，對我們家人來說亦同樣。」

亞洲協會的這場展覽，讓一位極具原創性、風格鮮明而充滿力量的畫家重新回到香港藝術界的視野。他留下的作品，見證了一段極其複雜的人生。

article_text:
mentor

劇場公開日： 2026年10月16日

解説・あらすじ

「ミッシング」「空白」「ヒメアノ～ル」の𠮷田恵輔が監督・脚本を手がけ、過去に囚われたまま大人になった2人の青年と、彼らの運命を狂わせていく「メンター（助言者）」の存在を描いた人間ドラマ。 ある日、龍之介と拓海という2人の少年の無邪気な花火遊びが、アパート火災を引き起こした。アパートは全焼し、巻き込まれた住人の埜本は妻子を失い自身も全身に火傷を負った。その日を境に、龍之介と拓海の時間は止まってしまう。15年後、龍之介は罪の意識に蓋をし、アーチェリーのオリンピック日本代表候補として前に進もうとしていた。その一方で、拓海は罪の記憶から抜け出せず、陰鬱な日々を過ごしていた。そんな2人の前に、埜本が突然姿を現す。2人に恨みの言葉をぶつけることもなく優しく接する埜本に、龍之介はどこか違和感を抱き、拓海は救いの光を見いだす。やがて埜本は、拓海にとって心の拠りどころとなるメンターのような存在となっていく。 「ヤクザと家族 The Family」「月」などの磯村勇斗が龍之介役、アイドルグループ「Aぇ！ group」のメンバーで本作が個人として初の映画主演となる末澤誠也が拓海役で主演を務め、物語の鍵を握るメンターの埜本役で綾野剛が共演。
